title: How much work: count before it grows
summary: A program that is quick on 100 lines can take hours on a million. Count how the work grows with the data, and measure.

scheme: find one name among n cards
a messy pile: look at each one   up to n
open the middle, keep one half  about log n
text: Before data grows, count the steps: how many times does the work run for n items?
- In a messy pile, you may look at every card: n steps.
- In sorted cards, each look throws away half: a million cards take about 20 looks.
- That's why paper dictionaries and database indexes keep things sorted.

scheme: two guest lists, n names each: who is on both?
each name against every name     n × n
sort both, walk them side by side
text: A loop inside a loop multiplies: for each name, read the whole other list again.
- 20 times more names on each side: 400 times more work.
- Sorted lists can be walked side by side, once each: far less work.
- It's the usual reason a script fine on a sample takes hours on the real file.

scheme: n          log n    n × log n     n × n
text: What counts is how the work grows, not how fast it is today.
- Programmers write it O(n), O(n²): "order n", "order n squared".
- On 100 items everything is fast. The difference shows only when data grows: plan for the real size.

scheme: time it on n lines, then on 2n
time × 2   grows like n (or n × log n)
time × 4   grows like n × n: look for
text: Don't guess, measure: time ./script big.txt, then on a file twice as big. Use inputs that take a few seconds, or start-up time hides the growth.
- Code an AI writes can hide a loop inside a loop: ask how the work grows with the data, then measure.
- The Logic path makes you find and fix one in a real script.
